name: Cyrus the Great
info: Cyrus II of Persia (c. 600 – 530 BCE), known as Cyrus the Great, founded the Achaemenid Empire by conquering Media, Lydia and Babylon, and is remembered for a policy of tolerance towards the customs and religions of conquered peoples.

facts.born: c. 600 BCE, son of Cambyses I, King of Anshan, and Mandane, daughter of Astyages, King of Media
facts.died: Around December 530 BCE; the accounts conflict: killed in battle with the Massagetae (Herodotus), with the Derbices (Ctesias) or with the Dahae (Berossus), or dead peacefully at his capital (Xenophon)
facts.role: King of Anshan from 559 BCE under Median overlordship; King of Persia and of Media after the fall of Ecbatana in 550 BCE; King of Babylon, King of Sumer and Akkad and King of the Four Corners of the World from 539 BCE
facts.known: Founding the Achaemenid Empire; the conquests of Media, Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire; the Cyrus Cylinder; the return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity; tolerance of local customs and religions; government through satraps; his tomb at Pasargadae

t: Cyrus began as a vassal king of Anshan under the Medes and by 550 BCE had overthrown his overlord and grandfather Astyages.
The conquests of Lydia and, in 539 BCE, of Babylon gave him the largest empire the world had seen to that point, stretching from Asia Minor to the Indus River.
Babylonian, Jewish and Greek sources remember him as a tolerant ruler, though historians read the Cyrus Cylinder as traditional royal propaganda and not as a charter of human rights.
dyk: The Book of Isaiah calls Cyrus anointed by Yahweh, a "messiah"; he is the only non-Jewish figure to be revered in this capacity.
ev: Cyrus is born to Cambyses I, King of Anshan, and Mandane, daughter of the Median king Astyages
He succeeds his father as king, still under Median overlordship
After at least three years of hostilities he captures Ecbatana and overthrows the Median kingdom
He defeats Croesus, occupies Sardis and conquers the Lydian kingdom
His army routs the Babylonians at Opis and he enters Babylon
He crosses the Hindu Kush and collects tribute from the Indus cities
He dies around December and is succeeded by his son Cambyses II

sections.early:
Cyrus was born during the period of 600–599 BCE to Cambyses I, King of Anshan, and Mandane, daughter of Astyages, King of Media. By his own account, now generally believed accurate, he was preceded as king by his father, his grandfather Cyrus I and his great-grandfather Teispes, who had taken the title "King of Anshan" after seizing that city. The traditional view holds that he was an Achaemenid, a descendant of Achaemenes, although M. Waters has suggested that his family was of Teispid and Anshanite origin and unrelated to the Achaemenids or to Darius the Great. Some scholars hold that his name, Kūruš in Old Persian, was Elamite in origin.

The story of his childhood is known from Herodotus, whose account is mythological. In it Astyages, warned by dreams that his grandson would supplant him, ordered the infant killed; his general Harpagus passed the task to a shepherd, who raised the boy as his own. When Cyrus was ten his royal birth was discovered and he was sent back to his parents in Persia, while Astyages punished Harpagus by tricking him into eating his own son. Strabo says that Cyrus was at first named Agradates.

Cyrus married Cassandane, an Achaemenian and daughter of Pharnaspes, who bore him two sons, Cambyses II and Bardiya, and three daughters, Atossa, Artystone and Roxane. When she died he insisted on public mourning throughout the kingdom; the Nabonidus Chronicle states that Babylonia mourned her for six days. On his father's death he inherited the Persian throne at Pasargadae, a vassal of Astyages.
sections.rise:
Cyrus succeeded to the throne in 559 BCE but, like his predecessors, had to recognise Median overlordship. Astyages may have ruled most of the Ancient Near East, from the Lydian frontier to the lands of the Parthians and Persians. According to the Nabonidus Chronicle, Astyages attacked Cyrus, "king of Ansan". Herodotus says that the Median commander Harpagus encouraged Cyrus to revolt and then defected with several nobles and part of the army, a mutiny the Chronicle confirms. The hostilities lasted at least three years (553–550 BCE) and ended with the capture of Ecbatana and of Astyages. According to Herodotus and Ctesias, Cyrus spared his grandfather's life and married his daughter Amytis. The Medes' vassals now came under his command, and the Chronicle records the change of his title from "King of Anshan" to "King of Persia".

The dates of the Lydian war are unknown, but it fell between 550 and 539 BCE. Croesus, king of Lydia, attacked the city of Pteria in Cappadocia and enslaved its inhabitants. Cyrus marched against him, and the Battle of Pteria was effectively a stalemate with heavy casualties on both sides. Croesus withdrew to Sardis and called on his allies, but before they could unite Cyrus besieged him there. At the Battle of Thymbra Harpagus advised placing dromedaries in front of the army, whose smell frightened the Lydian horses, and the Lydian cavalry was routed. Cyrus occupied Sardis in 546 BCE. Herodotus says he spared Croesus and kept him as an adviser; some translations of the Nabonidus Chronicle say the king of Lydia was slain.
sections.deeds:
After Lydia fell, a Lydian named Pactyas raised a revolt in Sardis. Cyrus sent Mazares, who subdued Magnesia and Priene, and then Harpagus, who took Lycia, Aeolia and Caria and finished the conquest of Asia Minor in 542 BCE. Between about 545 and 540 BCE Cyrus campaigned in the east, attacking Bactria, Arachosia, Sogdia, Chorasmia, Margiana and other regions, and in 533 BCE he crossed the Hindu Kush and collected tribute from the Indus cities.

By 540 BCE he had captured Elam and its capital, Susa. Just before October 539 BCE his army routed the Babylonians at Opis on the Tigris; Sippar was seized without a battle on 10 October, the general Gubaru's troops entered Babylon around 12 October and detained King Nabonidus, and Cyrus entered the city on 29 October. He proclaimed himself "king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, king of the four corners of the world" on the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder deposited in the foundations of the Esagila temple, which describes how he improved the lives of the Babylonians, repatriated displaced peoples and restored temples.

His dominions formed the largest empire the world had seen to that point, from Asia Minor to the Indus River. He governed it from four capitals, Pasargadae, Babylon, Susa and Ecbatana, allowing regional autonomy under satraps. The empire rested on tribute and conscripts; his army included the Immortals, a unit of 10,000 highly trained soldiers. He formed a postal system of relay stations, built palaces and irrigated gardens at Pasargadae, and made the Lydian Croeseid the standard gold coin of his empire.
sections.opponents:
Cyrus's enemies were the kings he displaced: Astyages of Media, Croesus of Lydia and Nabonidus of Babylon, whom the Cyrus Cylinder denounces as impious. Not every campaign succeeded: he was decisively defeated in Gedrosia, which was most likely conquered only under Darius I. Pactyas, who led the Lydian revolt, was probably tortured and put to death after his capture. In Herodotus's account the Massagetae queen Tomyris denounced as underhanded the stratagem by which Cyrus left wine to trap her son's troops.

Modern debate concerns his reputation for tolerance. The Shah of Iran presented the Cyrus Cylinder in the 1970s as "the first human rights charter in history"; others dispute this as "rather anachronistic", and the British Museum describes the cylinder as "an instrument of ancient Mesopotamian propaganda" in a long tradition of kings opening their reigns with declarations of reforms. Lester Grabbe maintains that his religious policy continued that of the Babylonians and Assyrians, and argues that there was no decree for the Jews' return but a general policy. Mary Joan Winn Leith writes that appeals to Marduk and to Yahweh show "the Persian tendency to co-opt local religious and political traditions in the interest of imperial control".

There was also Jewish criticism of Cyrus for halting the building of the Second Temple after the Cuthites accused the Jews of conspiring to rebel; it was not completed until 515 BCE. His own religion is uncertain: Pierre Briant calls it "quite reckless" to reconstruct it, and whether he was a Zoroastrian is debated.
sections.last:
The details of Cyrus's death vary by account. Herodotus has him die in battle with the Massagetae, a Scythian confederation, after their queen Tomyris rejected his offer of marriage and he tried to take her territory by force, about 529 BCE. Cyrus left a camp stocked with wine; Tomyris's son Spargapises and a third of her troops took it, drank and were defeated, and Spargapises killed himself in captivity. Tomyris then led a second force herself, Cyrus was killed in what Herodotus called the fiercest battle of his career, and she had his head dipped in a vessel of blood. Some scholars question this version, since Herodotus admits it was one of many he had heard.

Ctesias says that Cyrus died putting down resistance from the Derbices, north-east of the headwaters of the Syr Darya; Berossus, that he fell fighting the Dahae; and Xenophon's Cyropaedia, contradicting the others, that he died peacefully at his capital. Muhammad Dandamayev says the Persians may have recovered his body from the Massagetae. Cuneiform evidence from Babylon proves that he died around December 530 BCE and that his son Cambyses II had become king.

His remains may have been interred at Pasargadae, where a limestone tomb built around 540–530 BCE, which many believe to be his, still stands. Greek accounts describe a golden coffin inside it and Magi stationed to guard it. Cambyses captured Egypt but died after only seven years of rule. He was followed by Cyrus's other son Bardiya, or an impostor posing as him, who ruled for seven months until he was killed by Darius the Great.
sections.legacy:
The empire Cyrus founded reached its greatest extent under Darius the Great, and its system of many countries, religions and languages under one administration was retained by the Seleucids and by later Iranian dynasties, including the Parthians and Sasanians. According to Xenophon the peoples he ruled called him "The Father"; the Babylonians regarded him as "The Liberator". In Judaism he is exalted for ending the Babylonian captivity, and the Hebrew Bible credits his decree with the return to Zion and the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem.

Alexander the Great admired Cyrus from reading Xenophon's Cyropaedia. Finding the tomb at Pasargadae looted, he put its guardians on trial and ordered Aristobulus to restore it. The Cyropaedia was read by thinkers of the Renaissance and Enlightenment; Thomas Jefferson owned two copies. Charles Freeman suggests that Cyrus's achievements "ranked far above" those of Alexander, and Richard Nelson Frye writes that he "became the epitome of the great qualities expected of a ruler in antiquity".

In modern Iran he remains a cult figure. Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the last Shah, appealed to his legacy in celebrating 2,500 years of monarchy and adopted the Cyrus Cylinder, discovered in 1879 and now in the British Museum, as a political symbol. The tomb and Pasargadae are a UNESCO World Heritage site. From the 19th century some Indian Muslim scholars, first Syed Ahmad Khan and then Maulana Azad, identified Cyrus with Dhu al-Qarnayn of the Quran, a theory most Western scholars have not accepted.

summary: Cyrus II rose from vassal king of Anshan to master of Media, Lydia and Babylon, founding the Achaemenid Empire and ruling it through satraps. Ancient accounts disagree on how he died in 530 BCE. Babylonian, Jewish and Greek traditions remember him as a tolerant ruler, a reputation historians treat with caution.
references: Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (Eisenbrauns, 2002)
M. A. Dandamaev, A political history of the Achaemenid empire (Brill, 1989)
Irving Finkel, The Cyrus Cylinder: The Great Persian Edict from Babylon (I.B. Tauris, 2013)
Amélie Kuhrt, The Persian Empire: A Corpus of Sources from the Achaemenid Period (Routledge, 2013)

The article uses BC; I wrote BCE for the same years.
